scenarioA:
Use a coordinated cutover. The complete consumer inventory, approved outage, and supplied rehearsal evidence support a direct rename without maintaining duplicate columns.

1. Prepare matching schema and consumer changes. Verify database/tool-specific rename behavior, dependencies, locks, defaults, constraints and indexes. Before scheduling, run mandatory repository tests and schema checks, seeded migration tests verifying identical types and row-by-row values including nulls, and application/worker/report integration checks. Inspect actual execution and skips.
2. Stop every inventoried consumer, drain transactions, fence writes and prevent automatic restarts. Establish the recovery checkpoint.
3. Rename jobs.next_run to scheduled_at and deploy all matching consumers while stopped. Validate schema, preserved values and dependent objects; perform controlled checks before releasing writes.
4. Set a go/no-go deadline that reserves the rehearsed restore duration within 30 minutes. On failure, restore the checkpoint and compatible old consumers before writes resume. On success, restart only updated consumers, then monitor job scheduling and reports.

If a newly discovered report must keep reading next_run, the coordinated-consumer assumption fails. Retain a tested compatible interface at its actual query path—such as an appropriate database-supported alias or synchronized legacy column—until the report migrates. Reassess locking, recovery and timing, add that report to compatibility tests, and postpone removing next_run.

scenarioB:
Use expand–migrate–contract because old and new consumers must coexist continuously.

1. Inspect database/tool capabilities and consumer queries. Design an additive scheduled_at column with the same type, preserving next_run. Establish one authoritative write path and atomic synchronization covering old and new writers; application dual writes alone cannot cover unchanged old writers.
2. Run mandatory repository tests and schema checks. Test old/new consumer combinations, nulls, inserts and updates, concurrency, backfill races, recovery and representative production load. Confirm executed tests and inspect skips.
3. Add compatibility machinery using verified online DDL with bounded locking. Backfill in controlled batches without overwriting concurrent changes. Verify per-row equivalence and constraints while monitoring contention, latency and errors; stop rollout on drift or service degradation.
4. Roll out consumers gradually, retaining synchronization and next_run throughout the rollback window. Revert application versions against the compatible expanded schema if needed. The supplied 30-minute restore rehearsal does not establish uninterrupted recovery: restore requiring stopped writes is unsuitable here. Rehearse an online rollback or forward repair that preserves ongoing writes before rollout.
5. Remove next_run only after every old reader/writer is retired, the rollback window closes, and final compatibility/schema checks pass.

A newly discovered report that must read next_run extends the compatibility phase. Add it to the inventory and tests; defer contraction until it migrates.
